profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a tertiary academic hospital evaluating a draft clinical evaluation plan for a chest CT triage AI that flags suspected pulmonary embolism for radiologist prioritization. The proposal already exists as a 14-page protocol for hospital leadership review. The meeting is between the radiology clinical lead and the biostatistics/methods lead to judge whether the protocol is ready for submission to the hospital's digital health oversight committee. The agenda is to review the external testing section, the proposed reader study and prospective rollout evaluation, and the reporting checklist. The expected outcome is agreement on whether the protocol is 'submission-ready' and what minor revisions are needed before committee review.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Thoracic Radiologist and Clinical AI Lead
members.expertise: Chest imaging, radiology workflow integration, reader studies for diagnostic tools
members.background: Associate professor of radiology who has led several hospital pilots of imaging AI tools and helped implement a prior pneumothorax detection system in the emergency radiology service.
members.private_state: Wants the protocol to move forward this month so the vendor contract and internal pilot timeline are not delayed; is mainly concerned that the design looks clinically credible and operationally feasible to the oversight committee.
hidden_assumptions: If the protocol demonstrates the model on scans from the hospital's unaffiliated suburban campus, that counts as external testing because the workflow, scanners, and patient mix differ enough from the main academic site.

A prospective study for this kind of triage AI can mean a silent-run phase embedded in live operations before any randomized impact study, because what matters first is prospective data capture under real workflow conditions.

When the protocol says the design is ready for committee submission, it means the core logic, sample flow, and safety monitoring are stable, even if reporting details can be filled in during final manuscript preparation.
The prior PE triage pilot from two winters ago is the natural benchmark everyone has in mind when discussing the 'baseline workflow' and expected turnaround-time effects.

members.name: Dr. Vikram Shah
members.expertise: Diagnostic study design, pragmatic trials, reporting standards for AI evaluation, regulatory-grade evidence planning
members.background: Director of clinical research methods in the hospital's translational data science center, with experience advising on STARD-AI, SPIRIT-AI, and CONSORT-AI aligned study protocols.
members.private_state: Wants the protocol to withstand scrutiny from the oversight committee and future publication reviewers; is especially concerned about hidden methodological shortcuts that could make the evaluation look stronger than it is.
hidden_assumptions: External testing means performance assessment on data from an institution not involved in model development or threshold tuning; another campus in the same health system is still internal for methodological purposes.

A prospective study implies prospective allocation or at least pre-specified prospective evaluation of patient-level outcomes under the intended intervention, not merely a silent-run observational deployment.

A protocol is submission-ready only when reporting structure and prespecified analysis details are complete enough to map directly onto SPIRIT-AI or CONSORT-AI style expectations, because committees read these as signs of scientific maturity.

The 'baseline workflow' refers to the current standard reading process over the last six months after the recent worklist software upgrade, since older pilot-era workflow assumptions are no longer relevant.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the protocol includes 'external testing' before submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means testing on the suburban campus dataset within the same health system, using different scanners and a distinct patient population from the main site.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means testing on data from a separate institution entirely, with no shared development pipeline or threshold-setting decisions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are fluent in AI evaluation language and sincerely treat 'external testing' as a standard requirement, so the phrase creates false consensus; because the draft already names a second site, neither feels a need to unpack the institutional boundary implied by 'external'.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the design should include a 'prospective study' after the retrospective evaluation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a prospective silent-run phase in which the AI scores new chest CTs in real time without changing care, primarily to confirm operational performance and data capture in live workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a prospectively specified comparative intervention study, ideally randomized or at least paired under intended clinical use, to evaluate benefit of AI-assisted care versus conventional care.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In medical AI discussions, both silent-run and interventional studies are often described as prospective, so the term sounds safely shared; each hears the other's endorsement as support for their own familiar subtype.

misalignment_points.topic: What the review must cover before committee submission
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to making the protocol 'submission-ready' for the digital health oversight committee.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this review is about whether the evaluation design is clinically coherent and low-risk enough to go forward, with reporting checklists and some analysis wording polish handled afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes submission readiness includes near-final reporting architecture, prespecified subgroup handling, and explicit alignment to SPIRIT-AI/CONSORT-AI style items because those are part of design adequacy.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Design reviews commonly blend scientific design and documentation quality, and both members are accustomed to protocols evolving after review; the phrase 'submission-ready' sounds administrative rather than contested, so the scope difference remains latent.

misalignment_points.topic: Which baseline workflow is being compared
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to comparing AI-assisted reads against the 'baseline workflow' for turnaround-time and triage effects.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the preexisting PE triage pilot workflow from two winters ago, where radiologists manually monitored a flagged worklist and emergency cases were often batched.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the current post-upgrade workflow from the last six months, where the worklist software already auto-sorts urgent studies differently and turnaround-time distributions have shifted.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume there is one obvious baseline known to everyone on the project, and 'baseline workflow' sounds like a single shared operational fact; because they are discussing evaluation framing rather than operational details, neither specifies dates or software version.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to get over the line now. The committee mostly needs to see that the study is clinically sensible, safe, and operationally workable. The skeleton is there; we can polish checklist wording and manuscript-style detail later. If Vikram is basically on board, we can submit this month and avoid slowing the vendor timeline.

turns.inner_thought: I want to be careful here. 'Close' is fine, but if they send something half-specified, the committee will question the rigor immediately, and reviewers certainly would later. I need to go section by section: external testing, prospective study, and whether the protocol reads like a mature evaluation plan rather than a concept note.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'd like to walk through the external testing plan, the prospective study section, and then whether the protocol is complete enough to be genuinely submission-ready for oversight review.

turns.inner_thought: The external testing argument is one of the stronger parts already. The suburban campus is outside the main academic workflow, with different scanner mix, referral patterns, and patient throughput. For clinical audiences, that absolutely demonstrates the model generalizes beyond the exact environment where it was first tuned.
turns.utterance: On the external testing piece, I actually think we're in pretty good shape already. We have the evaluation on the suburban campus scans, and that gives us a distinctly different scanner mix and patient flow from the main hospital, which should read as a meaningful external testing cohort.

turns.inner_thought: Good, external testing is in there at least. I still need the write-up to make very clear how the external cohort is kept separate from development and threshold-setting; otherwise it will look hand-wavy. If that separation is documented crisply, the committee may accept it for now even though I would still want stronger evidence later.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree that external testing is essential here. I think the main improvement would be to tighten the wording so the committee can see clearly how that external cohort is separated from development and how it functions in the overall evidence sequence.

turns.inner_thought: He seems satisfied, good. Next, the prospective study is already covered by the eight-week live silent run. That gives us real-time data capture, integration checks, and operational confidence without changing care. For this stage, that's exactly what we need before activation discussions.
turns.utterance: And on the next section, I do want to emphasize that the protocol already includes a prospective study after the retrospective evaluation. The system will run live in the background for eight weeks before any clinical activation, so we'll have prospective data under real workflow conditions.

turns.inner_thought: Good, they are at least thinking prospectively. But the protocol needs to make explicit what the comparison will be when AI is actually used and how benefit versus conventional care will be assessed. A prospective study should not stop at observational logging if they want claims about impact.
turns.utterance: I agree that having a prospective study is important. What I'd recommend is making the comparison framework more explicit so it's clear how the eventual benefit of AI-assisted care versus conventional care will be evaluated.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine; I can frame it around operations. The main thing the committee will recognize is the turnaround-time endpoint relative to the baseline workflow, just like in the PE triage pilot everyone remembers. That should make the rationale feel familiar and low risk.
turns.utterance: Right, and the main operational endpoint in the draft is the change from the baseline workflow in time-to-first-radiologist-review, which I think will be very familiar to the committee from prior PE triage work.

turns.inner_thought: That endpoint is reasonable, but they need to anchor baseline workflow to the current standard process, not legacy pilot assumptions. Since the worklist upgrade changed urgent routing and turnaround distributions, any comparison has to describe that carefully or the estimate will be misleading.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. I would just describe the baseline workflow very carefully, because the current standard routing has already changed some urgent-case timing patterns, and the committee may look closely at how that comparison is defined.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want this turning into a full rewrite. If the core design passes, my team can add the SPIRIT-style polish later. The oversight committee is not waiting for a journal-ready protocol; they need a coherent plan now so procurement and pilot scheduling don't slip.
turns.utterance: Understood. My view is that if the core design is acceptable now, I can have the team clean up the checklist language and expand some of the reporting details after the committee discussion. I mainly want to avoid holding submission while we do cosmetic polishing.

turns.inner_thought: This is the key point. For me, submission-ready includes the reporting architecture, not just the concept. If the main analyses, subgroup handling, and AI-specific reporting elements are vague now, that is a design problem, not mere cosmetics. I need to push gently without sounding obstructive.
turns.utterance: I hear you, though for something to be submission-ready I would be more comfortable if the protocol already mapped the main analyses, subgroup handling, and the key reporting items more explicitly. Those details tend to signal scientific maturity to reviewers, including internal ones.

turns.inner_thought: He wants more structure, but it still sounds like we're aligned on the essentials. If I summarize the shared pieces—external testing, prospective study, baseline workflow, and some write-up polish—we can keep momentum and avoid reopening fundamentals.
turns.utterance: That's fair. It sounds like we're aligned on keeping the external testing site, the prospective study phase, and the baseline workflow comparison, while making the write-up more explicit so the submission-ready version reads cleanly for the committee.

turns.inner_thought: We're close enough that I can work through comments rather than block the process outright. I still want stronger definitions in the text, but if I annotate the external testing language, the prospective study section, and the reporting structure, maybe we can get it to an acceptable standard before submission.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think it's close. I'll send annotated comments today so the submission package reflects those same elements clearly for review, especially around the external testing description, the prospective study section, and the analysis and reporting structure.
